message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference Guide to Its Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium, 99.98 %), H‑2 (deuterium, 0.02 %), H‑3 (tritium, ~10⁻⁵ %) |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 1 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| **Physical Properties** | State at STP | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.9 °C (20.3 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.2 °C (14.0 K) |
| | Density (STP) | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume (STP) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat (gas, 25 °C) | 28.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.449 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Refractive index (visible) | 1.000132 |
| | Viscosity (25 °C) | 1.52 µPa·s |
| | Surface tension (25 °C) | 0.0028 N m⁻¹ |
| **Chemical Properties** | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | First ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, etc. |
| | Bond dissociation energy (H–H) | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Acidic strength | Very weak acid (HF is the strongest H‑acid) |
| | Basicity | Very weak base (hydride ion H⁻ is a strong base) |
| | Flammability | Extremely flammable; explosive in air (1–4 % H₂ in air) |
| | Combustion reaction | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (ΔH ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Hydrogen bonding | H₂O, HF, NH₃ exhibit strong H‑bonding; H₂ itself does not |
| **Isotopic Differences** | Deuterium (²H) | 2 × mass of protium; heavier, lower zero‑point energy, stronger bonds |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β⁻ decay, t½ ≈ 12.32 y); used in radiolabeling and fusion research |
| **Nuclear & Astrophysical** | Abundance in Universe | ~75 % of baryonic mass; most abundant element |
| | Role in stars | Fusion of H into He powers stars; proton‑proton chain, CNO cycle |
| | Fusion reaction (pp‑chain) | 4 p → ⁴He + 2 e⁺ + 2 νₑ + 26.7 MeV |
| | Fusion reaction (CNO cycle) | 4 p + ¹²C → ¹²C + 4 e⁺ + 4 νₑ + 26.7 MeV |
| | Hydrogen in cosmology | Residual H after Big Bang nucleosynthesis; 21‑cm line probes early Universe |
| **Applications & Uses** | Fuel cell technology | H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (electrochemical) |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid H₂ + liquid O₂ (LH₂/LOX) |
| | Metallurgy | Reducing agent for iron ore, steelmaking |
| | Chemical synthesis | Hydride reagents (LiAlH₄, NaBH₄), hydrogenation of alkenes |
| | Medical imaging | Deuterated water (D₂O) in NMR, tritiated water in tracer studies |
| | Energy storage | Hydrogen storage in metal hydrides, high‑pressure tanks, cryogenic liquefaction |
| **Safety & Handling** | Explosion limits in air | Lower flammability limit 4 %, upper 75 % |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic; inhalation can cause hypoxia due to displacement of oxygen |
| | Storage temperature | Cryogenic (–253 °C) for liquid form; high pressure (~700 bar) for gas |
| | Corrosion | Can embrittle metals (hydrogen embrittlement) |

---

### Quick Takeaways

1. **Hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element** – a single proton and one electron.
2. **It exists mainly as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions, but its isotopes (deuterium, tritium) have distinct physical and nuclear properties.
3. **Its chemical behavior is dominated by its ability to form covalent bonds** (H–H, H–O, H–C, etc.) and its role as a reducing agent or fuel.
4. **In astrophysics, hydrogen fusion powers stars** and drives the evolution of the Universe.
5. **Practical uses span from fuel cells to rocket propellants**, but handling requires careful control of flammability and pressure.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
